title: He shouldn’t have been in the story.
paragraphs: He shouldn’t have been in the story.

Not like that.
Not from that kind of night.
And yet—his name made it into eternity.
Perez.

You almost skip him.
You almost ignore the chapter.
You almost pretend Genesis 38 isn’t there.
But God didn’t skip it.
And that’s where this gets uncomfortable… and powerful.
Because Perez was born out of a moment soaked in failure→restoration.

Judah—his father—was not walking in righteousness.
He failed his responsibility.
He neglected justice.
He drifted.
Tamar—his mother—was caught in a desperate situation, forced into a decision that still makes readers pause.
This is not a clean story.

It’s messy.
Complicated.
Morally heavy.

And if we’re honest—
it feels a little too close to home.
Because not all of our stories are clean either.
Some of us carry chapters we don’t talk about.

Moments we wish weren’t recorded.
Decisions made in pressure, loneliness, or quiet rebellion.
Failures that echo in our minds when everything gets silent.
You look at your past and think:

“God can’t use this.”
“God won’t touch this.”
“This part disqualifies me.”
But Perez is standing in Scripture like a contradiction to that lie.
Listen carefully.

Genesis 38:29 (ESV):
"What a breach you have made for yourself!" Therefore his name was called Perez.
“Breach.”
Breaking through.
Out of confusion… something broke through.
Out of failure… something still came forward.
Out of a situation that looked disqualified… God allowed a future to be born.
Let that sit.
Because we think failure ends the story.

God says—
“I can start something in the middle of it.”
But don’t miss this.
The Bible does not celebrate the sin.
It exposes it.

Judah’s failure had consequences.
The situation was not God’s design.
Sin always leaves damage.

Romans 6:23 says:
"For the wages of sin is death..."
That’s real.

Sin destroys.
Sin fractures.
Sin leaves weight in the soul.
So this is not a story of “it’s okay.”
This is a story of God stepping into what is not okay.
And here’s where the tension breaks open into glory.
Perez—this overlooked, uncomfortable, “we don’t talk about that chapter” child—
was placed in the lineage of Jesus Christ.
Let that hit your chest.

Matthew 1:3 (ESV):
"Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar..."
God didn’t edit the scandal out.
He wrote it in.

Not to glorify sin—
but to magnify grace.
Some scholars interpret this genealogy as intentionally raw—God showing that the Messiah came through broken human history, not sanitized perfection.
Jesus did not come from a flawless line.
He came through real people.

Flawed.
Wounded.
Complicated.
People like Judah.
People like Tamar.
People like you.
And here’s the Gospel—clear, unfiltered, unshakable:
You are not saved by having a clean story.
You are saved by a crucified Savior.
Jesus Christ stepped into our broken humanity, lived the life we could not live, and died the death we deserved.

2 Corinthians 5:21 (ESV):
"For our sake He made Him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God."
Do you see it?
Your failure does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
But there is a response.
Grace is not permission to stay the same.
Grace is an invitation to repent and be transformed.
Judah’s story didn’t end in failure—later, you see glimpses of change, humility, and responsibility (Genesis 44).

Failure does not have to define you—
but it must lead you somewhere.
To repentance.
To surrender.
To Christ.
Because without repentance, failure becomes a cycle.
But with Christ—failure becomes a doorway.
A breach.
A breaking through.
Some of you are stuck staring at your worst moment like it’s your final identity.
God is saying:
“That’s not the end of your name.”
Perez didn’t choose the circumstances of his birth.
But God chose his future.
And here’s the truth you need to hear—without softening it:

Your sin is real.
Your failure matters.
You are accountable.
But your story is not beyond redemption.
Not because you are strong.
But because Jesus is sufficient.

Romans 5:20 (ESV):
"Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more."
Not equal.
More.
Grace doesn’t just meet sin.
It overflows it.
So what are you doing with the part of your life you keep hiding?

That secret?
That failure?
That regret you replay at night?
Bring it into the light.
Not later.
Now.

1 John 1:9 (ESV):
"If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Faithful.

Not hesitant.
Not reluctant.
Faithful.
You don’t clean yourself up and then come to God.
You come to God—and He cleanses you.
Perez is proof.

God can take what started in failure
and weave it into redemption.

God can take a chapter you’re ashamed of
and place His grace right in the middle of it.

God can take a name you think is disqualified
and write it into His purpose.
But you have to come.
Not hiding.
Not pretending.
Not delaying.
Come broken.
Come honest.
Come repentant.
Come to Jesus.
And watch what grace does with what you thought was the end.
Pause.
Let God deal with you.
